To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the HIV‐1 quasispecies in children and their infected mothers are genetically very similar, (ii) the viral populations in the children are more divergent than the viral populations in their mothers, (iii) the viral populations of the children and their mothers are genetically similar to each other and to the viral populations of other HIV‐1 infected individuals, (iv) the HIV‐ 1 populations in children are more diverged than the populations of other HIV ‐1 infected individuals,
HIV‐1 evolves to a more diverse population with time and that this diversity increases in the absence of antiretroviral therapy.
the diversity of the HIV-1 quasispecies in the mother is higher and more variable than that in the child.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new technologies to detect and characterize the genetic diversity of viral populations in the context of HIV‐1 infection.
the evolution of viral populations in the human host.
the development, selection, and evolution of human behavior.

the virus is a complex and dynamic entity and that the evolution of the viral quasispecies is a complex process that is affected by the host and by the environment, including the treatment.
the virus evolves and diversifies over time and that the evolution of the viral populations is not random, but follows a pattern.

HIV‐1 is a highly diverse virus, with an enormous capacity to mutate and adapt to the changing environment, and that the virus is capable of producing a large number of different quasispecies in each infected individual.

the viral quasispecies is highly diverse, with a high degree of divergence, and that the viral populations evolve in a complex manner, with the emergence of variants in the viral population that are able to replicate and persist in the face of selective pressures.
